summary.text: For an odd prime \(p\mid n=pt\) with \(t\ge2\), counting the factors \(2^{jd}-1\) for \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\mid p-1\) and comparing their \(p\)-adic contribution with the valuation of \((pt-1)!\) shows \(p\mid a(n-1)\); the hypothesis would force \(p\mid2^{n-2}\), so a composite \(n\) could only be \(2^v\), which is excluded by the exact calculation \(v_2(a(2^v-1))=v-1\). Thus \(n\) is prime, and if \(d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2)<n-1\), then \(n\mid2^d-1\), a factor in the numerator for \(a(n-1)\), forcing \(n\mid a(n-1)\) since \(n\nmid(n-1)!\), a contradiction; hence \(d=n-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(m)=\frac{2^{m-1}}{m!}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1)\qquad(m\ge 1).
\]
For convenience, put
\[
 P_m=\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1),\qquad N_m=2^{m-1}P_m,
\]
so that we will have the exact identity
\[
 a(m)m!=N_m. \tag{1}
\]
We first justify this identity and establish the valuation facts needed later.

Throughout, for a prime \(q\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in a positive integer \(x\).

### 1. Preliminary divisibility and valuation facts

We use the standard factorial estimate
\[
 (q-1)v_q(r!)<r \qquad(r\ge1). \tag{2}
\]
This follows, for example, from Legendre's formula
\[
 v_q(r!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac r{q^j}\right\rfloor:
\]
the corresponding geometric series is strictly less than \(r/(q-1)\). Since the quantities are integers, (2) implies
\[
 v_q(r!)\le \left\lfloor\frac{r-1}{q-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{3}
\]
In particular,
\[
 v_2(r!)\le r-1. \tag{4}
\]

We next record how odd-prime powers occur in \(P_m\). Let \(q\) be an odd prime and let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)
\]
be the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(q\). Since \(2\not\equiv0\pmod q\), this order is positive. Fermat's theorem gives \(2^{q-1}\equiv1\pmod q\), and hence
\[
 d\mid q-1. \tag{5}
\]
Also, by the definition of the order,
\[
 q\mid 2^d-1. \tag{6}
\]
For every positive integer \(j\), (6) implies
\[
 q\mid 2^{jd}-1,
\]
either directly from \(2^d\equiv1\pmod q\), or from the factorization \(x^j-1=(x-1)(x^{j-1}+\cdots+1)\).

There are exactly
\[
 M=\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{d}\right\rfloor
\]
positive multiples \(d,2d,\ldots,Md\) not exceeding \(m-1\). The corresponding \(M\) distinct factors of \(P_m\) are all divisible by \(q\). Therefore
\[
 q^M\mid P_m,
\]
or equivalently
\[
 v_q(P_m)\ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{d}\right\rfloor. \tag{7}
\]

We can now prove that the displayed formula for \(a(m)\) is always integral. For \(q=2\), every factor \(2^k-1\) in \(P_m\) is odd, while \(N_m\) contains the factor \(2^{m-1}\). Thus
\[
 v_2(N_m)=m-1\ge v_2(m!)
\]
by (4). For an odd prime \(q\), (5) gives \(d\le q-1\), so (7) and (3) give
\[
 v_q(N_m)\ge v_q(P_m)
 \ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{d}\right\rfloor
 \ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{q-1}\right\rfloor
 \ge v_q(m!).
\]
Thus every prime occurs in \(N_m\) to at least the exponent with which it occurs in \(m!\). Hence \(m!\mid N_m\), proving that \(a(m)\) is an integer and proving the exact identity (1). Notice also that \(P_m\), \(N_m\), and \(a(m)\) are positive for every \(m\ge1\).

### 2. An odd prime divisor lemma

We prove the following central assertion:

> If \(p\) is an odd prime and \(t\ge2\), then
> \[
> p\mid a(pt-1). \tag{8}
> \]

Set
\[
 m=pt-1
\]
and let \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\). As above, \(d\mid p-1\), so \(d\le p-1\). By (7),
\[
 v_p(N_m)\ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{d}\right\rfloor
 \ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{9}
\]
Now
\[
 m-1=pt-2=t(p-1)+(t-2),
\]
and consequently
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 =t+\left\lfloor\frac{t-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{10}
\]
Thus
\[
 v_p(N_m)\ge t+\left\lfloor\frac{t-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{11}
\]

We compare this with the valuation of \(m!\). Since
\[
 m=pt-1=p(t-1)+(p-1),
\]
the integers strictly after \(p(t-1)\) and at most \(m\) are
\[
 p(t-1)+1,\ldots,p(t-1)+(p-1),
\]
none of which is divisible by \(p\). Hence
\[
 v_p(m!)=v_p((p(t-1))!).
\]
Among the factors of \((p(t-1))!\), the multiples of \(p\) are \(p,2p,\ldots,(t-1)p\). Removing one factor \(p\) from each of them leaves the product \((t-1)!\). Therefore
\[
 v_p(m!)=(t-1)+v_p((t-1)!). \tag{12}
\]
Applying (3) with \(r=t-1\), which is positive because \(t\ge2\), gives
\[
 v_p((t-1)!)\le \left\lfloor\frac{t-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{13}
\]
Combining (12) and (13),
\[
 v_p(m!)\le (t-1)+\left\lfloor\frac{t-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{14}
\]
Comparison of (11) and (14) shows
\[
 v_p(N_m)\ge v_p(m!)+1.
\]
Using \(N_m=a(m)m!\) and additivity of valuations, we conclude \(v_p(a(m))\ge1\). This proves (8).

### 3. The power-of-two case

We will also need to show that no power of \(2\) greater than \(2\) can satisfy the divisibility in the conjecture.

Let \(v\ge2\), set
\[
 n=2^v,\qquad m=n-1=2^v-1.
\]
We first calculate \(v_2(a(m))\). Every factor of \(P_m\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(N_m)=m-1=2^v-2. \tag{15}
\]
Legendre's formula gives the exact value
\[
 v_2((2^v-1)!)=2^v-1-v. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, for \(1\le j\le v-1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{2^v-1}{2^j}\right\rfloor=2^{v-j}-1,
\]
and all terms with \(j\ge v\) vanish. Therefore
\[
 v_2((2^v-1)!)
 =\sum_{j=1}^{v-1}(2^{v-j}-1)
 =(2^v-2)-(v-1)
 =2^v-1-v.
\]
Subtracting (16) from (15) in the identity \(N_m=a(m)m!\), we obtain
\[
 v_2(a(2^v-1))=v-1. \tag{17}
\]

On the other hand, for \(v\ge2\) one has
\[
 2^v-2\ge v. \tag{18}
\]
For instance, equality holds at \(v=2\), and the inequality is preserved and strengthened when \(v\) is increased by one. It follows that
\[
 2^v\mid 2^{2^v-2}. \tag{19}
\]
Suppose, contrary to what we want, that
\[
 2^v\mid a(2^v-1)+2^{2^v-2}.
\]
By (19), subtracting the second summand shows that \(2^v\mid a(2^v-1)\). This would imply
\[
 v_2(a(2^v-1))\ge v,
\]
contradicting (17). We have therefore proved
\[
 2^v\nmid a(2^v-1)+2^{2^v-2}\qquad(v\ge2). \tag{20}
\]

### 4. The assumed divisibility forces \(n\) to be prime

Now let \(n>2\) and assume
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{21}
\]
We first show that if an odd prime \(p\) divides \(n\), then in fact \(n=p\).

Write \(n=pt\). If \(n\ne p\), then \(t\ne1\). Also \(t\ne0\), since \(n>2\). Thus \(t\ge2\). The odd-prime divisor lemma (8) gives
\[
 p\mid a(pt-1)=a(n-1). \tag{22}
\]
Because \(p\mid n\), assumption (21) also gives
\[
 p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{23}
\]
Subtracting (22) from (23), we find
\[
 p\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
A prime dividing a positive power of \(2\) must divide \(2\), so \(p=2\), contrary to the assumption that \(p\) is odd. Therefore every odd prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\) satisfies \(n=p\). In particular, if \(n\) has an odd prime divisor, then \(n\) is prime.

Suppose now, for contradiction, that \(n\) is composite. By the preceding paragraph, it cannot have an odd prime divisor: an odd prime divisor would have to equal \(n\), making \(n\) prime. Thus every prime divisor of \(n\) is \(2\). By unique factorization,
\[
 n=2^v
\]
for some integer \(v\ge0\). Since \(n>2\), necessarily \(v\ge2\). But then (21) becomes
\[
 2^v\mid a(2^v-1)+2^{2^v-2},
\]
contradicting (20). This contradiction proves that
\[
 n\text{ is prime}. \tag{24}
\]
Since \(n>2\), it is an odd prime.

### 5. The order of \(2\) modulo \(n\)

It remains to prove that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Put
\[
 m=n-1.
\]
We first claim that
\[
 n\nmid a(m). \tag{25}
\]
If instead \(n\mid a(m)\), then (21) would imply, after subtraction, that
\[
 n\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
Since \(n\) is prime, it would follow that \(n\mid2\), which is impossible for the odd prime \(n>2\). Thus (25) holds.

From the exact defining identity (1),
\[
 a(m)m!=N_m
 =2^{m-1}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1). \tag{26}
\]
We claim that
\[
 n\nmid N_m. \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, if \(n\mid a(m)m!\), primality of \(n\) would imply that \(n\mid a(m)\) or \(n\mid m!\). The first alternative contradicts (25). The second is also impossible, because \(m=n-1\), so every factor in \(m!=1\cdot2\cdots(n-1)\) is positive and strictly less than the prime \(n\); equivalently, \(v_n((n-1)!)=0\). This proves (27).

Let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2).
\]
Because \(n\) is an odd prime, \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(n\), so \(d>0\). Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 d\mid n-1, \tag{28}
\]
and by definition of the order,
\[
 n\mid 2^d-1. \tag{29}
\]
We show that \(d=n-1\). If not, then (28), positivity of \(d\), and \(d\ne n-1\) imply
\[
 1\le d<n-1=m.
\]
Thus the factor \(2^d-1\) appears among the factors in
\[
 P_m=\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1).
\]
By (29), \(n\mid2^d-1\), hence \(n\mid P_m\), and therefore \(n\mid N_m=2^{m-1}P_m\). This contradicts (27). Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_n(2)=n-1. \tag{30}
\]

Finally, because \(n\) is prime, Euler's totient is \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Equation (30) says exactly that the residue class of \(2\) has order \(\varphi(n)\) in the multiplicative group modulo \(n\): it satisfies \(2^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n\), and whenever \(2^\ell\equiv1\pmod n\), its order \(n-1\) divides \(\ell\). Hence \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

We have proved that every \(n>2\) satisfying
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
is prime and has \(2\) as a primitive root modulo \(n\), as required.
